summary.title: Impact of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesion Length on Six-month Angiographic and 2-year Clinical Outcomes
summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon W Rha
summary.executive_summary: This study investigated whether lesion length in chronic total occlusion (CTO) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) affects outcomes in the drug-eluting stent (DES) era. A prospective cohort of 235 patients from a single center in South Korea was divided into long (≥30mm) and short (<30mm) CTO groups. Baseline characteristics showed that the long CTO group had more prior PCI and intimal dissection, while the short CTO group had more bifurcation lesions. At six months, angiographic outcomes including binary restenosis and late loss were statistically similar between groups, though numerical trends favored the short group. Over two years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including death and myocardial infarction, did not differ significantly. However, the long CTO group exhibited a significantly higher incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs 7.8%, p < 0.05), driven primarily by target vessel revascularization (TVR). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26, 95% CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesions are associated with higher rates of repeat revascularization, they do not translate into worse hard clinical endpoints like mortality or MI within two years. Limitations include the single-center design, lack of randomization, and reliance on physician discretion for follow-up angiography.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigated whether lesion length in chronic total occlusion (CTO) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) affects outcomes in the drug-eluting stent (DES) era. A prospective cohort of 235 patients from a single center in South Korea was divided into long (≥30mm) and short (<30mm) CTO groups. Baseline characteristics showed that the long CTO group had more prior PCI and intimal dissection, while the short CTO group had more bifurcation lesions. At six months, angiographic outcomes including binary restenosis and late loss were statistically similar between groups, though numerical trends favored the short group. Over two years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including death and myocardial infarction, did not differ significantly. However, the long CTO group exhibited a significantly higher incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs 7.8%, p < 0.05), driven primarily by target vessel revascularization (TVR). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26, 95% CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesions are associated with higher rates of repeat revascularization, they do not translate into worse hard clinical endpoints like mortality or MI within two years. Limitations include the single-center design, lack of randomization, and reliance on physician discretion for follow-up angiography.

Research Context
Successful CTO PCI is linked to improved clinical outcomes compared with failed attempts. Despite DES advancements, long coronary lesions remain a poor prognostic factor after PCI. CTO procedural success rates remain lower than non-CTO patients, influenced by baseline lesion characters. There are no definite answers regarding CTO PCI outcomes based on lesion length in the DES era.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine if CTO lesion length impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes. Hypothesis: Long CTO lesions will result in worse angiographic and clinical outcomes compared to short lesions. Predicted outcomes include higher rates of restenosis, MACE, and repeat revascularization in the long CTO group. The study predicts that newer generation DES usage might differ between groups, affecting outcomes.

Methodological Details
The study enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients who underwent successful PCI with DESs. Patients were recruited from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital. The cohort was divided into long CTO (≥30mm, n=159) and short CTO (<30mm, n=76) groups. CTO was defined as complete obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0 and duration ≥3 months. Only de novo lesions were included; in-stent restenosis was excluded from the analysis. All patients received dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel post-procedure. Clopidogrel administration was encouraged to continue for at least one year. PCI procedures utilized standard techniques with various guidewires and simple pre-dilation. Procedural success was defined as diameter stenosis <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. Follow-up data was collected via face-to-face interviews, medical record review, or telephone contact. Statistical analysis used Student's t-test for continuous variables and χ2 for categorical variables. Logistic regression adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, CKD, prior PCI, and bifurcation. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.

Procedures And Architectures
Quantitative coronary angiographic (QCA) parameters were measured before, immediately after, and at 6 months. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis assessed at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included in-stent restenosis, mean diameter stenosis, and late loss. The primary clinical endpoint was Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE) at two years. MACE included total death, recurrent myocardial infarction, and revascularization (PCI or CABG). Secondary clinical endpoints included death, MI, repeat PCI, TLR, TVR, and non-TVR. Deaths were classified as cardiac unless non-cardiac death could be confirmed. T-L-MACE was defined as cardiac death, MI, and target lesion revascularization. TVR-MACE was defined as the composite of cardiac death, MI, and target vessel revascularization. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20 software.

Key Results
Baseline characteristics were similar except prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group. Bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group compared to the long group. In-hospital complications were similar except intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Six-month angiographic outcomes including ISR and binary restenosis were not different between groups. Binary restenosis showed a numerical trend favoring the short group (8.8% vs 19.1%, p=0.12). Late loss was 0.65 mm in the long group vs 0.46 mm in the short group (p=0.13). Two-year MACE incidence was 21.3% in the long group vs 13.1% in the short group (p=0.13). Total death rates were 3.1% in the long group vs 5.2% in the short group (p=0.43). Cardiac death rates were 1.2% in the long group vs 2.6% in the short group (p=0.45). Myocardial infarction rates were 1.8% in the long group vs 2.6% in the short group (p=0.71). Repeat PCI incidence was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs 7.8%, p < 0.05). Target vessel revascularization was significantly higher in the long CTO group (16.3% vs 6.5%, p < 0.05). Long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI with OR 4.26 (95% CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006). Long CTO was an independent predictor for TVR with OR 4.23 (95% CI 1.52-11.8, p < 0.05). Vessel diameter was smaller in the short group (2.92 mm) vs long group (3.11 mm, p < 0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Long CTO lesions are associated with higher repeat PCI rates but not worse hard endpoints. The higher TVR rate in long CTO did not translate into increased mortality or cardiac death. Less myocardial viability and developed collaterals may lessen the physiologic effect of restenosis. Numerical trends in binary restenosis suggest potential long-term risks not fully captured in 2 years. Vessel diameter differences were insufficient to significantly affect angiographic or clinical outcomes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is not randomized and is a single-center registry with prospective data collection. Baseline clinical, lesion, and procedural characteristics were slightly different between the two groups. Use of newer generation DES was frequent in the short group, while first-generation stents were common in the long group. Unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could exist despite strict statistical adjustment. Follow-up angiography was not routine and depended on symptoms or physician discretion. Physician discretion for follow-up angiography may introduce confounders related to collateral development. The sample size was relatively small, limiting power to prove differences in angiographic events. The two-year follow-up period may not be long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Multivariate analysis adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, CKD, prior PCI, and bifurcation.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrated baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics of the two groups. Table 2 showed procedural and in-hospital complications, including intimal dissection. Table 3 summarized clinical outcomes for the two-year follow-up period. Table 4 showed predictors for repeat PCI and TVR from logistic regression. Table 5 presented six-month angiographic outcomes including ISR and binary restenosis.

Three Takeaways
1. Long CTO lesion length is an independent predictor for repeat PCI and TVR. 2. Despite higher repeat PCI, long CTO does not increase hard endpoints like mortality within two years. 3. Larger, long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings and assess long-term safety.
